title: How a Tiny Chip Turns Electricity into Light

segments.text: Can a grain‑sized chip replace a lamp?
A light‑emitting diode is a semiconductor that glows when current flows.
Electrons recombine with holes and release photons.
The band‑gap energy decides the photon’s color.
Early LEDs only gave faint infrared, then low‑intensity red.
Modern LEDs cover infrared, visible, and ultraviolet wavelengths.
They power traffic signals, aircraft lights, and camera flashes.
Because they convert electricity directly to light, they switch extremely fast, which enables advanced communications.
That fast, direct conversion lets a tiny chip replace many traditional light sources.
